parsed.title: Discussion on AI tools, job search, and code generation risks

topics.title: Automation of job search and resume generation

claims.text: User P1 is preparing for a full‑time job search and wants to set up cloud tools for automated PDF resume generation per vacancy.
P1 plans to configure OpenClaw to find vacancies, generate resumes and cover letters once the startup closes.
P1 believes lacking AI‑related skills (LLM, RAG, embeddings, etc.) will cause recruiters to filter them out in 2026.
P1 states that the acceleration of development started in 2025, with tools becoming both better and more expensive.

topics.title: Impact of AI on recruiting and hiring

claims.text: P1 predicts the recruiter profession will die out and HR will become just personnel management.
P4 remarks that keyword‑based candidate search is increasingly detached from reality.
P4 comments that nothing has fundamentally changed over time.
P2 describes using GPT to auto‑generate SQL joins, which speeds up development but can produce unsafe, heavy queries.
P1 shares an example where AI generated a 450‑line raw SQL query that pulls all user data, leading to potential security and performance issues.
P1 recounts a incident where a teammate pushed SELECT * to production after AI generated code, causing project instability.
P4 notes that incremental computations have been replaced by materialized views (implying a shift due to AI code patterns).

topics.title: Use of logs and debugging practices

claims.text: P2 suggests that analyzing logs (e.g., in JMH) could have helped earlier detection of recurring issues.
P4 argues that a well‑configured environment and accumulated context are more valuable than raw logs for problem solving.
P2 acknowledges that logs would not have helped much in their current situation.

topics.title: Quality of AI answers vs question quality

claims.text: P4 observes that answer quality often correlates with question quality and the amount of auxiliary knowledge available to the system.
